name: Shellfish gathering, Pinnacle Point, South Africa
summary: People at Pinnacle Point on South Africa's south coast were eating shellfish and other sea foods about 164,000 years ago, the earliest well-dated case when reported.
description: Excavations at cave 13B at Pinnacle Point, near Mossel Bay, show that by about 164,000 years ago (give or take 12,000 years) people on the south coast of South Africa had widened their diet to include shellfish and other marine foods, perhaps in response to harsh glacial conditions. The team called it the earliest dated observation of this behaviour, the earliest previous evidence being about 125,000 years old.

impact.note: Shore foods extended foraging to a new and dependable food for people of one coast; wider consequences, such as coastal routes out of Africa, are suggested and not demonstrated in the sources read.

date.label: c. 164,000 years ago
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The excavation's leader states that at 164,000 years ago (about 162,050 BCE) people in coastal South Africa expanded their diet to include shellfish and other marine resources.

evidence.supports: Our findings show that at 164,000 years ago in coastal South Africa humans expanded their diet to include shellfish and other marine resources, perhaps as a response to harsh environmental conditions

date.label: c. 164,000 years ago (±12,000)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Marean and colleagues date the widening of the diet at Pinnacle Point, on the south coast of South Africa, to include marine resources to about 164,000 years ago, with a stated error of 12,000 years either way (about 174,050–150,050 BCE).

evidence.supports: Here we show that by ∼164 kyr ago (±12 kyr) at Pinnacle Point (on the south coast of South Africa) humans expanded their diet to include marine resources

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Only the abstract of the 2007 Nature paper was read; the full paper should be opened for the dated layers and the shellfish counts.
Whether shellfish collection was timed to the spring tides was not checked.
Other early claims of shellfish use, such as Benzú rock shelter in North Africa, were not checked and bear on first_known.
The coordinates are for the promontory and need checking against a gazetteer.

research.note: The 2007 Nature report says the earliest previous evidence of marine resource use dated to about 125,000 years ago. A 2011 study of Bajondillo Cave, Spain, dates Neanderthal shellfish use to about 150,000 years ago and calls it almost contemporaneous with Pinnacle Point, where it says shellfishing is first documented, so the priority holds only within dating error.
